Namola

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
We often hear how long it takes police to respond to a 10111 emergency call, and this was recently highlighted in the Van breda case. This is all set to change with a product called Namola, a free app for all citizens - it enables them to connect directly with crime fighting authorities. Similar to UBER, press the emergency button, the the closet three police calls will respond to your co-ordinates, and within 90 seconds a place car will get to you. no need to give your name or address. it should revolutionaries the way we report criminal activity or get help for ourselves in immediate danger. it’s been developed by Happimo a non profile organization which sources develops and deploys social uplifting apps. We plan to show how it works , where its being used at the moment, its full roll out plan and also to test it - how fast will a police car arrive after we push the emergency number.

Press Release:


Namola
A crime fighting solution right at your fingertips? A locally designed and tested app could soon become the solution to crime. Using smart phone
technology, Namola allows users to alert the nearest police officers when they need assistance and promises to reduce emergency response
times, down to as little as 90 seconds. Carte Blanche puts it to the test

Script:


Delays in police and ambulance responses can start with a call to an emergency center.

This was so dramatically illustrated when an audio recoding of murder accused Henri van Breda was played out in court. In Jan last year he called an emergency center to request urgent help for his family he claimed was attacked by an ax wilding intruder.

UPSOUND

The call took an astonishing 25 minutes to establish his location while his parents and brother lay dead, and his sister clinging to life. And there was more (confusion) when the ambulance service joined the call.

UPSOUND

LINK: Well that type of scenario might soon be a thing of the past. An app has been developed which will drastically reduce police response times and its hoped make a significant impact in the fight against crime.

An innovative crime fighting app called Namola has been designed to allow citizens - via their gps enabled smart phones - to share their physical addresses and receive an immediate response.

LINK: You know an app is likely to be successful when you wonder why it hasn’t been always being around even if the idea comes from an unlikely place. The namola app was born after a very informal conversation between friends over a beer.


The discussion centered around crime, police and emergency response times. Craig Rivett who headed up Happimo, an npo which develops socially uplifting apps, remembers that evening.

Craig: One thing we realized is that you know the way we respond to crime hasn’t changed much over the last 2 decades. We still use a radio network. We still use sort of telephone lines and the big problem we have here is we have got 11 official languages. The delays don’t come from the police driving, the delays come from getting your information to a control room, to the officer and out.

Allan Knott Craig, well known SA entrepreneur, was part of that discussion. It was he who came up with the idea of a crime fighting app. He contacted mobile tech guru peter Matthaei.

John: What was your reaction to that call?
Peter: From Alan I trust these kinds of ideas. Its not because people mostly have bad ideas. It's just because I know of all the difficulties there are in launching a successful app in South Africa.


But this free app was bound to success! Think uber - but for crime fighting.

John: Actually if you consider uber as the template, its almost a perfect fit?
Peter: Yes, boil uber down to it...uber basically says I am here, this is my location and this is the service I need. You don’t have to say much else. Its just I am here and I am in need.

Craig and his team went to work. They launched a pilot with the enthusiastic Tshwane metro police dog unit in Feb. 2015.

Craig: There were some incredible guys on the ground who were dedicated, they were there everyday. When we were trying to promote this app, they were out taking brochures to shops to people there. They were wanting to drive for change.


Following the success of the pilot, the city of Tshwane financed the further development of Namola. It went live march 2015. 230 Tshwane metro police cars were fitted with Namola enable tablets. On the 11th of may, Namola reach was expanded when it was officially launched in Gauteng, in partnership with the Gauteng department of community safety and the Gauteng traffic police.

One person who can vouch for namola is Irfaan Majam whose security company was guarding taxi ranks. He was working in Soweto when a gang of heavily armed men approached

Irfaan: Then about 14 guys came with 3 R1s, 2 R5s, 1 AK.
John: Really?
Irfaan: And handguns and the rest of my team was at the other taxi rank. There was only 3 of us.

He hit the app’s emergency button and then spoke to operators who immediately contacted the police.

Irfaan: I was actually surprised that day because the cops came in about 2 minutes and they came with a squad bro. We talking about special tactical forces that came in 2 minutes. I mean I could have been dead if it wasn’t because of yous.

Another key to the apps success is it could lessen the number of hoax calls. Recently the minister of police Fikile Mbalula visited visited a 101111 call center and heard that up to 70 per cent of calls were hoaxes. Crime activist Yusuf Abramjee says that this can all change now.

Yusuf: Through Namola the minute you press the button, your profile appears on the screen in the control room with your photograph, your name, your address and it gives you the locations.

With their identity and location known, no doubt pranksters will think twice. Abramjee is adamant Namola is the future.

Yusuf: Well I think it has got great potential. I think it is going to make a difference. It is making a difference already. Everyone that has tested the App will tell you what a quick response you get.

It was time to test namola. We chose a quite street in albertyn.

Link: So I have just witnessed a crime. I have my smart phone in my hand and I have opened the app and I push this button. George Raftopolis from the Gauteng traffic service or traffic police is here to keep time. Start the clock

My location and details immediately popped up on a screen in the namola control room. Operators immediately sent my gps coordinates to police cars patrolling a few kilometers from where I stood.

John: And any second now a call should come through from the control center just asking what the nature of the crime is and to let me know that a vehicle is on the way but I can hear sirens in teh background so I already know that help is on route.

John: George time wise how are we looking?
George: 30 seconds now.
John: Great here comes a call. Lets have a word with the control center.
Hi this is John from Carte Blanche.
Operator: Hi john, its Suren from Namola. What is your emergency?
John: I have just witnessed a crime. This is a controlled experiment but we understand that vehicles are already on route.
John: Time wise George how we looking?
George: One and half minutes here come the vehicles...and stop the clock.

Just over a minute and a half. Very impressive. Traffic officers seems genuinely excited about the potential of Namola.

John: Siphiwe earlier on I said to you that this app could become a game changer and you said that it already is.
Siphiwe: Absolutely it is game changer. Unlike the normal radio that we have been using. I think the app itself and the device in the vehicle gives us more time to respond much faster than on the radio. Especially when a person is in distress.

John: Siphiwe sometimes the police get a bad wrap and obviously sometimes it is warranted and sometimes not but how do you think this app is likely change how you approach your job?
Siphiwe: As a law enforcement officer I mean this is what I do, do you understand. I’m passionate about what I am doing and getting to people faster is actually pleasing to me.

Namola is currently in advanced discussions with emergency 101111 centers to integrate with their systems. At this stage Namola is “live” in Gauteng but it seems only a matter of time before other provinces come aboard.

Peter: Everyday my inbox is just full of users from north west, from cape town from bloem, kzn. From all over the countries users are on my case that we need to bring this service to the whole of South Africa. When are we going to be there?
